title: George (23 April)
hook: a soldier-martyr whose dragon is a legend, patron of England and other lands

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stanislaus, struck down after he told a king no. Your line was the bishop of kraków. Did you find the other telling of a story? Day nine hundred eighty-three.

A red cross on a white field, flying over a stadium in England. A knight on a horse, spearing a dragon, on a gold coin, a church window, a pub sign. A painted icon in an Orthodox church, the same young rider, the same twisting beast under his hooves. The man in all of them is George. Yet the dragon is the part tradition added later. Behind the horse and the spear stands a much plainer story: a soldier, and a choice. Today, the man under the legend.
screen: `A RED CROSS, A KNIGHT, A DRAGON.` → `THE DRAGON CAME LATER.` → `A SOLDIER, AND A CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Here is what tradition holds about George himself. He was a soldier in the Roman army in the east, a Christian, at a time when an emperor ordered Christians to sacrifice to the gods. George would not. He was tortured and put to death, and Christians began to honor his grave. Beyond that, the details are thin, and the Church is frank about it. An early Church decree, long credited to a pope, counted him among saints whose names people rightly honor but whose deeds are known only to God. Then the dragon. In a medieval collection of saints' lives called the Golden Legend, a dragon terrorizes a city, demanding victims, until the lot falls on the king's daughter. George rides up, wounds the beast in the name of Christ, and the princess leads it into the city on her own sash. The people ask for baptism. It's a legend, and a beloved one, told and painted across Europe and the Christian East. The Church holds both pieces: the martyr, whose feast the Church keeps, and the legend, which is free to be what it is, a picture. Saint Paul gives the same picture without the scales. In the Douay-Rheims: "Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil." The dragon in the story stands for evil. The real George's dragon was an order he would not obey. England, Georgia, Catalonia and other places took him as patron. The legend gave him a beast. The refusal is the part the oldest tellings already hold.
screen: `A SOLDIER WHO WOULD NOT SACRIFICE.` · `HIS DEEDS KNOWN ONLY TO GOD.` · `THE DRAGON: A MEDIEVAL LEGEND.` · `HIS REAL DRAGON WAS AN ORDER.` · then, large: `PUT YOU ON THE ARMOUR OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face one dragon. Settle, and breathe. Name one dragon in your own life. Not a monster, maybe. A habit that eats your evenings. A fear you feed to keep it quiet. A demand you keep giving in to. A conversation you keep dodging. Look at it plainly, the way George looked at the order he would not obey. You don't need to slay it today. Just name it, and choose one small first move against it. If you pray, you can ask for courage, perhaps with the Our Father's line, deliver us from evil. If you don't, just hold your one move steady. The bell holds the time.
George. A soldier martyred for refusing to sacrifice to the gods, whose dragon is a medieval legend, honored as patron of England and other places.
Your line: slay the dragon. Today, make your one small first move against the dragon you named. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint George's optional memorial on 23 April; in England it is a feast, and Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians honor him as a great martyr with icons of the rider and the dragon.

notes: Audit: 'the part that is plainly his' overstated what can be known (the Church itself says his deeds are thin); softened. Also confirm whether 23 April is a feast or a solemnity in England and Wales before howItsDone ships.
Claims rule: no dates or counts spoken (Diocletian's persecution, year of death). Emperor not named.
'An early pope counted him among saints whose names people rightly honor but whose deeds are known only to God': the Decretum Gelasianum, attribution to Gelasius disputed. Confirm phrasing.
Patronage named: England, Georgia, Catalonia, 'and other places'. Confirm.
Golden Legend details (lot falls on the king's daughter, wounded dragon led on her girdle/sash, baptism of the city) paraphrased; confirm.
Practice quotes 'deliver us from evil' from the Our Father (Matthew 6:13) without a translation source; confirm acceptable as the liturgical line.
